MetaCheck Report

A Multilevel Signal Detection Theory Approach to Unconscious Processing Research

2026-11-22 · Metacheck 0.4.4.29 · DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24019945

5to fix2to check0to decide by hand0fine8not applicable

To fix (5)

To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

Comparing these classifications with the actual experimental conditions quantifies the kind of classifications that participants are asked to perform in typical awareness tasks, and provides the binary responses needed for any conventional SDT analysis.

Figure 4 shows the estimates of the multilevel model for the two samples discussed in the section “Challenges for the Correlation and Intercept Hypotheses”, in which each participant completed 80 (Panel A) or 20 (Panel B) trials per task.

Under the model of Klauer et al. (1998), the multilevel SDT model accurately recovered both the population correlation and intercept, despite the violation of its assumed bivariate normal distribution, and even though up to 80% of participants had a true awareness-task sensitivity of exactly zero.

In the subsequent conditioning test (influence task), CS-US pairings were randomized and conditioning was measured as 𝑑 ′ (e.g., a “pleasant” response counted as a hit when preceded by “NPLW” and as a false alarm when preceded by “DHJF”, regardless of whether the word itself was pleasant or unpleasant).

Eighty-six participants completed 360 trials per task, equally balanced between conditions.

After the search task, participants completed an explicit recognition test (awareness task), identifying Old and New displays using a six-point confidence scale, allowing awareness to be assessed using both 𝑑 ′ and rating-based measures.

Each participant completed 384 visual-search trials across 24 blocks (192 Old and 192 New), followed by 64 recognition trials (32 Old and 32 New), with responses ranging from 1 (“sure New”) to 6 (“sure Old”).

To make this assumption more plausible,Reingold and Merikle (1988) recommended that the two tasks be as similar as possible, differing mainly in whether participants are explicitly asked to discriminate the relevant information.

To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 2 potential power analyses.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8’ to check the contents of 8 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: effect_size, effect_size_metric, software

power_id power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
1 apriori one-sample t-test 30 0.05 0.8 NA other NA
2 apriori other 40 0.05 0.8 NA NA other
power_id text
1 Power of a one-sample t test (𝛼 = .05) for 30 participants. Both tasks are assumed to have the same true effect size, expressed in terms of signal-detection sensitivity (𝑑 ′ ), which provides a common metric for comparing effects across different measures, as we explain below. Shaded bands mark typical numbers of trials in each task; the dotted line marks 80% power.
2 Power to Detect Sensitivity Differences as a Function of Awareness-Task Number of Trials Note. Power of the difference between mean sensitivities in the multilevel SDT model (𝛼 = .05), computed with the usdt_power() function of {uSDT} for a sample of 40 participants. True mean sensitivities were 0.30 (awareness) and 0.15 (influence), with between-participant SDs of 0.15 and a population correlation of zero between tasks. Trials per condition ranged from 3 to 100 (awareness) and were fixed at 150 (influence). The open circle marks the minimum number of awareness-task trials required to reach 80% power (dotted line) SDT models, see Rouder & Lu, 2005; Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013). This extension is relatively straightforward and is already implemented in the {uSDT} package: the model structure remains unchanged, but prior distributions are assigned to its parameters. Combining these priors with the observed trial-level likelihood yields posterior distributions for all model parameters, including the five population parameters defining our three hypotheses. These posterior distributions can be used to compute credible intervals and, with appropriate prior specifications, Bayes factors to quantify evidence for or against the null hypotheses (Dienes, 2014; Wagenmakers, 2007).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 6 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 504 of 6838 data columns (7%) are documented in a codebook; 6334 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (6 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 7% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents task, primeset, targ_set while the data has subj, file, trial. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 3 codebook/README/label sources and 6838 data columns across 530 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (6 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 7% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents task, primeset, targ_set while the data has subj, file, trial. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

Duplicated Column Names

  • Duplicated column names in Results/Simulation studies/Processed/validation_emmeans_tables.rdata. 1 column name appears more than once (worst: value×7), so 7 of the file’s 9 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

To fix Repository Check

What we found

  • We found 797 files in 3 repositories.
  • We did not check 2 linked deposits that are not this paper’s own: https://osf.io/ydeza (others’ data); https://osf.io/9t4pk (others’ data).
  • We found 3 README files and 1 repository without READMEs.
  • The manuscript’s studies and the repository’s file groups do not match.
  • We found 12 file naming problems to fix.
  • We left out 41 files that do not belong in a repository: open-document lock files (1), operating system (40). Remove them from the repository.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the repository separates out a study (ex3) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 12 naming problems that should be fixed, and 379 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 41 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: open-document lock files (1), operating system (40). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).

Missing Files

All other files loaded in the code were present in the repository. 22 files the code reads are not in the repository, but the code downloads or unpacks files without naming them (such as osf_download() or unzip()), so they may be made by it and are not counted as missing: exp1_data.RData, exp2_data.RData, exp3_data.RData, exp4_data.RData, experiment_1B_no_load.csv, experiment_2.csv, multiverse_rt_A3A4.csv, multiverse_aw_B2.csv, multiverse_aw_A3.csv, figure_aw_multiverse_B2.RData.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 2 code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 6 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 28 distinct packages/libraries: afex, dplyr, effectsize, emmeans, ggplot2, gridExtra, haven, httr, kableExtra, knitr, lme4, logspline, metafor, minqa, numDeriv, osfr, patchwork, psychmeta, R.matlab, remotes, scales, SimDesign, tibble, tidyr, tidyverse, tools, uSDT, utils. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

The repository holds MATLAB code. State the version of MATLAB used in the README, and list any add-ons the code needs (for Stata, the user-written commands installed with ssc install; for MATLAB, the toolboxes), so that readers can run the code with the same software.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 797 files: 542 data, 85 code, 32 documentation, 136 materials, 2 unknown.
  • We found 542 tabular data files and extracted 6838 columns from 530 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 5 study groups (ex1, ex1c, ex2, ex2a, ex3), plus 2 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 6 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass local_path to point at a local copy. We ran automated data-quality checks on 6838 columns; 474 columns have at least one potential issue (327 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 62 columns whose values look like personal information; 56 columns whose names become identical when special characters are removed; 27 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 4 columns with numeric values stored as text).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 6838 columns across 530 data files.

Issues Identified

474 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 530 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 50 scripts: 7 ran without error, 25 errored, 7 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 7 were run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 4 scripts need the internet, which is off during the run: 1. greenwald2017_prepare_data.R, 26_generate_multiverse_VGLV23_20240710.R, 01_download_data.R, R scripts/Empirical illustrations/4. wentura2025_exp2a_analysis.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. 2 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded: uSDT_robustness_analysis.R, uSDT_validation_analysis.R. They are not counted as scripts that did not reproduce. The files: uSDT_pub_zenodo/Results/Simulation studies/Raw/Robustness study/uSDT_robustness_simres.rds (252.7 MB), uSDT_pub_zenodo/Results/Simulation studies/Raw/Validation study/uSDT_validation_simres.rds (452.9 MB); files over 100 MB are not downloaded.

Calls that install packages in the code

7 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Run by another script

7 scripts are run by another script with source(), so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

> ci_dz <- function(dz, n, level = .95) {
>   t_obs <- dz * sqrt(n)
>   df <- n - 1
>   a <- (1 - level) / 2
> 
>   cdf <- function(ncp) {
>     integrate(function(v) {
>       pnorm(t_obs * sqrt(v / df) - ncp) * dchisq(v, df)
>     }, 0, Inf, rel.tol = 1e-9)$value
>   }
> 
>   ncp <- sapply(c(1 - a, a), function(p) {
>     uniroot(function(ncp) cdf(ncp) - p,
>             c(t_obs - 10, t_obs + 10), tol = 1e-8)$root
>   })
> 
>   ncp / sqrt(n)
> }
> ci_r <- function(r, n, level = .95) {
>   tanh(atanh(r) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(1 - (1 - level) / 2) / sqrt(n - 3))
> }

> num_iterations <- 200
> raw_data <- rbind(read.csv("data_exp_B1_rt.csv"), read.csv("data_exp_B2_rt.csv"))
> main_df <- data.frame(epoch_1 = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
>                       epoch_2 = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
>                       epoch_3 = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
>                       epoch_4 = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
>                       log_RTs = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
>                       cutoff  = c(2, 2.5, 3),
>                       stat    = c("mean", "median", "learning rate"))
> main_df <- tidyr::expand(main_df, epoch_1,epoch_2,epoch_3,epoch_4,log_RTs,cutoff,stat)
> main_df <- subset(main_df, (epoch_1|epoch_2|epoch_3|epoch_4))
> main_df <- subset(main_df, stat!="learning rate"|(epoch_1&epoch_2&epoch_3&epoch_4))
> main_df$spec_id <- 1:nrow(main_df)
> main_df <- main_df[rep(seq_len(nrow(main_df)), each=num_iterations), ]
> main_df$split_half_r <- 999999
> randomize_trials <- function(df){
>   df$trial <- sample(1:nrow(df))
>   df <- df[order(df$subj, df$epoch, df$pattId, df$trial),]
>   df$trial <- 1:nrow(df)
>   return(df)
> }
> for (n in 1:nrow(main_df)){
>   
>   # track progress...
>   if (n%%100==0){print(paste("spec:", n, "/ progress:", round(100*n/nrow(main_df), digits=2), "%"))}
> 
>   # by default data for specification n is equal to raw_data
>   data_n <- raw_data
>   max_rt <- 10000
> 
>   # assign random trial numbers...
>   data_n <- randomize_trials(data_n)
>   
>   # depending on log RT...
>   if (main_df$log_RTs[n]==TRUE){
>     data_n$rt <- log(data_n$rt)
>     max_rt <- log(max_rt)
>   }
>   
>   # filter trials...
>   cutoff <- main_df$cutoff[n]
>   data_n <- filter_rts(data_n, max_rt, cutoff)
>   data_n <- subset(data_n, valid.trial==1)
>   
>   # depending on epochs...
>   if (main_df$epoch_1[n]=="FALSE"){data_n <- data_n[!data_n$epoch==1,]}
>   if (main_df$epoch_2[n]=="FALSE"){data_n <- data_n[!data_n$epoch==2,]}
>   if (main_df$epoch_3[n]=="FALSE"){data_n <- data_n[!data_n$epoch==3,]}
>   if (main_df$epoch_4[n]=="FALSE"){data_n <- data_n[!data_n$epoch==4,]}
>   
>   # split data set...
>   data_n_1 <- subset(data_n, trial%%2!=0)
>   data_n_2 <- subset(data_n, trial%%2==0)
>   
>   # depending on statistic (mean/median/learning rate)...
>   if (main_df$stat[n]=="mean"){
>     m_1 <- compute_cc_mean(data_n_1)$cuing
>     m_2 <- compute_cc_mean(data_n_2)$cuing
>   } else if(main_df$stat[n]=="median") {
>     m_1 <- compute_cc_median(data_n_1)$cuing
>     m_2 <- compute_cc_median(data_n_2)$cuing
>   } else if(main_df$stat[n]=="learning rate") {
>     m_1 <- compute_cc_learning_rate(data_n_1)$cuing
>     m_2 <- compute_cc_learning_rate(data_n_2)$cuing
>   }
>   
>   # compute split-half correlation...
>   split_half <- cor(m_1, m_2)
> 
>   # store results of iteration...
>   main_df$split_half_r[n] <- split_half
>   
> }

> Summarise <- function(condition, results, fixed_objects) {
>   Attach(condition)
>   # True values. The intercept estimate is compared with the hsdt intercept
>   # of the population (intercept) and with the model's own (alpha)
>   truth <- c(mu_dD = mu_dD, mu_dI = mu_dI, mu_cD = mu_cD, sd_dD = sd_dD,
>              sd_dI = sd_dI, sd_cD = sd_cD, cov_d = cov_d, diff = diff,
>              rho = cor_d, intercept = intercept_hsdt, slope = slope_hsdt,
>              alpha = intercept)
> 
>   # Bias, relative bias and RMSE over the replications with an estimate;
>   # coverage and MSRSE over those with CI and SE
>   recovery <- unlist(lapply(names(truth), function(p) {
>     q   <- if (p == "alpha") "intercept" else p
>     est <- results[[paste0(q, "_est")]]
>     se  <- results[[paste0(q, "_se")]]
>     CIs <- cbind(results[[paste0(q, "_lo")]], results[[paste0(q, "_hi")]])
>     ok    <- !is.na(est)
>     se_ok <- ok & !is.na(se)
>     ci_ok <- complete.cases(CIs)
>     res <- c(bias        = if (any(ok)) bias(est[ok], truth[[p]]) else NA,
>              rel_bias    = if (any(ok) && truth[[p]] != 0) bias(est[ok], truth[[p]], type = "relative") else NA,
>              RMSE        = if (any(ok)) RMSE(est[ok], truth[[p]]) else NA,
>              coverage    = if (any(ci_ok)) ECR(CIs[ci_ok, , drop = FALSE], truth[[p]]) else NA,
>              MSRSE       = if (sum(se_ok) > 1) MSRSE(cbind(se[se_ok]), cbind(est[se_ok])) else NA,
>              missing_est = mean(!ok),
>              missing_ci  = mean(!ci_ok))
>     setNames(res, paste0(p, "_", names(res)))
>   }))
> 
>   # Rejection rates of the three hypotheses over the testable replications
>   # (type I error when the truth is zero, power otherwise)
>   rejection <- sapply(c("diff", "rho", "intercept", "slope"), function(p) {
>     pv <- results[[paste0(p, "_p")]]
>     if (any(!is.na(pv))) EDR(pv[!is.na(pv)], alpha = .05) else NA
>   })
>   names(rejection) <- paste0(names(rejection), "_rejection")
> 
>   # Boundary: singular fits, hypotheses without SE (not testable), and which
>   # variance is estimated at zero or correlation at +-1
>   boundary <- c(
>     singular      = mean(results$singular, na.rm = TRUE),
>     untestable_H1 = 1 - mean(results$testable_H1),
>     untestable_H2 = 1 - mean(results$testable_H2),
>     untestable_H3 = 1 - mean(results$testable_H3),
>     zero_sd_dD    = mean(!is.na(results$sd_dD_est) & results$sd_dD_est < 1e-4),
>     zero_sd_dI    = mean(!is.na(results$sd_dI_est) & results$sd_dI_est < 1e-4),
>     zero_sd_cD    = mean(!is.na(results$sd_cD_est) & results$sd_cD_est < 1e-4),
>     one_rho       = mean(!is.na(results$rho_est) & abs(results$rho_est) > 1 - 1e-6))
> 
>   # Convergence
>   fits <- c(failed    = mean(results$failed),
>             converged = mean(results$converged, na.rm = TRUE),
>             time_fit  = mean(results$time_fit))
> 
>   c(recovery, rejection, boundary, fits)
> }

> Generate <- function(condition, fixed_objects) {
>   Attach(condition)

>   d_I <- intercept + slope * d_D + rnorm(N, 0, sd_res)
> 
>   # Direct criterion (indirect criterion fixed at zero, as after Meyen's split)
>   c_D <- rnorm(N, mu_cD, sd_cD)
> 
>   # Hit and false-alarm counts of each task, in the format of usdt_data_tasks
>   direct <- data.frame(
>     subj      = rep(1:N, 2),
>     condition = rep(c("signal", "noise"), each = N),
>     yes       = c(rbinom(N, trials, pnorm( d_D / 2 - c_D)),
>                   rbinom(N, trials, pnorm(-d_D / 2 - c_D))),
>     n         = trials)
>   indirect <- data.frame(
>     subj      = rep(1:N, 2),
>     condition = rep(c("signal", "noise"), each = N),
>     yes       = c(rbinom(N, trials, pnorm( d_I / 2)),
>                   rbinom(N, trials, pnorm(-d_I / 2))),
>     n         = trials)
> 
>   dat <- list(direct = direct, indirect = indirect)
>   dat
> }
> Analyse <- function(condition, dat, fixed_objects) {
>   # Data in uSDT format
>   d <- uSDT::usdt_data_tasks(
>     direct           = dat$direct,
>     indirect         = dat$indirect,
>     subject_col      = "subj",
>     condition_col    = "condition",
>     condition_levels = c(signal = "signal", noise = "noise"),
>     successes_col    = "yes",
>     trials_col       = "n",
>     successes_type   = "counts")
> 
>   # TEMPORARY: hsdt() only fixes the indirect criterion at zero when uSDT did
>   # Meyen's split itself, so the flag is set by hand
>   d$meta$criterion_zero[["indirect"]] <- TRUE
> 
>   # Estimate multilevel SDT model
>   time_fit <- system.time({
>     fit <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(uSDT::hsdt(d))),
>                     error = function(e) NULL)
>   })
> 
>   # Estimate, SE, CI and p value of each parameter. A failed fit keeps NA, so
>   # that it is counted instead of replaced by new data
>   pars <- c("mu_dD", "mu_dI", "mu_cD", "sd_dD", "sd_dI", "sd_cD", "cov_d",
>             "diff", "rho", "intercept", "slope")
>   out  <- matrix(NA_real_, length(pars), 5,
>                  dimnames = list(pars, c("est", "se", "lo", "hi", "p")))
> 
>   # Diagnostics. singular is lme4's boundary (singular) fit warning; a
>   # hypothesis is testable only if it has SE and CI
>   diagnostics <- c(failed = 1, converged = NA, singular = NA,
>                    testable_H1 = 0, testable_H2 = 0, testable_H3 = 0)
> 
>   if (!is.null(fit)) {
>     z <- qnorm(.975)
> 
>     # Fixed effects (the criterion is fitted with the opposite sign)
>     out[c("mu_cD", "mu_dD", "mu_dI"), "est"] <-
>       lme4::fixef(fit$fit)[c("c_D", "d_D", "d_I")] * c(-1, 1, 1)
>     out[c("mu_cD", "mu_dD", "mu_dI"), "se"]  <-
>       sqrt(diag(as.matrix(vcov(fit$fit))))[c("c_D", "d_D", "d_I")]
> 
>     # Random-effect SDs
>     re <- fit$pars$re
>     out[c("sd_cD", "sd_dD", "sd_dI"), "est"] <- re$sd[match(c("c_D", "d_D", "d_I"), re$term)]
>     out[c("sd_cD", "sd_dD", "sd_dI"), "se"]  <- re$se[match(c("c_D", "d_D", "d_I"), re$term)]
> 
>     # Covariance between sensitivities
>     out["cov_d", "est"] <- fit$pars$est[["s_DI"]]
>     out["cov_d", "se"]  <- suppressWarnings(sqrt(fit$pars$vcov["s_DI", "s_DI"]))
> 
>     # Wald CIs and p values (log scale for SDs, as in summary.hsdt)
>     wald <- c("mu_cD", "mu_dD", "mu_dI", "cov_d")
>     sds  <- c("sd_cD", "sd_dD", "sd_dI")
>     out[wald, "lo"] <- out[wald, "est"] - z * out[wald, "se"]
>     out[wald, "hi"] <- out[wald, "est"] + z * out[wald, "se"]
>     out[wald, "p"]  <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(out[wald, "est"] / out[wald, "se"]))
>     out[sds, "lo"]  <- exp(log(out[sds, "est"]) - z * out[sds, "se"] / out[sds, "est"])
>     out[sds, "hi"]  <- exp(log(out[sds, "est"]) + z * out[sds, "se"] / out[sds, "est"])
> 
>     # Three hypotheses
>     tests <- fit$tests[match(c("d'(indirect) - d'(direct)", "correlation",
>                                "intercept", "slope"), fit$tests$term), ]
>     out[c("diff", "rho", "intercept", "slope"), ] <-
>       as.matrix(tests[, c("estimate", "se", "conf.low", "conf.high", "p.value")])
> 
>     diagnostics <- c(failed      = 0,
>                      converged   = fit$diagnostics$converged,
>                      singular    = fit$diagnostics$singular,
>                      testable_H1 = tests$status[1] %in% "ok",
>                      testable_H2 = tests$status[2] %in% "ok",
>                      testable_H3 = tests$status[3] %in% "ok")
>   }
> 
>   # Return results: <parameter>_<statistic>, diagnostics and time
>   res <- c(setNames(c(t(out)), paste(rep(pars, each = 5), colnames(out), sep = "_")),
>            diagnostics,
>            time_fit = time_fit[["elapsed"]])
> 
>   # Return results
>   return(res)
> }
> Summarise <- function(condition, results, fixed_objects) {
>   Attach(condition)
>   # True values
>   truth <- c(mu_dD = mu_dD, mu_dI = mu_dI, mu_cD = mu_cD, sd_dD = sd_dD,
>              sd_dI = sd_dI, sd_cD = sd_cD, cov_d = cov_d, diff = diff,
>              rho = rho, intercept = intercept, slope = slope)
> 
>   # Bias, relative bias and RMSE over the replications with an estimate;
>   # coverage and MSRSE over those with CI and SE
>   recovery <- unlist(lapply(names(truth), function(p) {
>     est <- results[[paste0(p, "_est")]]
>     se  <- results[[paste0(p, "_se")]]
>     CIs <- cbind(results[[paste0(p, "_lo")]], results[[paste0(p, "_hi")]])
>     ok    <- !is.na(est)
>     se_ok <- ok & !is.na(se)
>     ci_ok <- complete.cases(CIs)
>     res <- c(bias        = if (any(ok)) bias(est[ok], truth[[p]]) else NA,
>              rel_bias    = if (any(ok) && truth[[p]] != 0) bias(est[ok], truth[[p]], type = "relative") else NA,
>              RMSE        = if (any(ok)) RMSE(est[ok], truth[[p]]) else NA,
>              coverage    = if (any(ci_ok)) ECR(CIs[ci_ok, , drop = FALSE], truth[[p]]) else NA,
>              MSRSE       = if (sum(se_ok) > 1) MSRSE(cbind(se[se_ok]), cbind(est[se_ok])) else NA,
>              missing_est = mean(!ok),
>              missing_ci  = mean(!ci_ok))
>     setNames(res, paste0(p, "_", names(res)))
>   }))
> 
>   # Rejection rates of the three hypotheses over the testable replications
>   # (type I error when the truth is zero, power otherwise)
>   rejection <- sapply(c("diff", "rho", "intercept", "slope"), function(p) {
>     pv <- results[[paste0(p, "_p")]]
>     if (any(!is.na(pv))) EDR(pv[!is.na(pv)], alpha = .05) else NA
>   })
>   names(rejection) <- paste0(names(rejection), "_rejection")
> 
>   # Boundary: singular fits, hypotheses without SE (not testable), and which
>   # variance is estimated at zero or correlation at +-1
>   boundary <- c(
>     singular      = mean(results$singular, na.rm = TRUE),
>     untestable_H1 = 1 - mean(results$testable_H1),
>     untestable_H2 = 1 - mean(results$testable_H2),
>     untestable_H3 = 1 - mean(results$testable_H3),
>     zero_sd_dD    = mean(!is.na(results$sd_dD_est) & results$sd_dD_est < 1e-4),
>     zero_sd_dI    = mean(!is.na(results$sd_dI_est) & results$sd_dI_est < 1e-4),
>     zero_sd_cD    = mean(!is.na(results$sd_cD_est) & results$sd_cD_est < 1e-4),
>     one_rho       = mean(!is.na(results$rho_est) & abs(results$rho_est) > 1 - 1e-6))
> 
>   # Convergence
>   fits <- c(failed    = mean(results$failed),
>             converged = mean(results$converged, na.rm = TRUE),
>             time_fit  = mean(results$time_fit))
> 
>   c(recovery, rejection, boundary, fits)
> }
> global_seeds <- genSeeds(design = Design, iseed = 2026)
> res <- runSimulation(
>   design         = Design,
>   replications   = 1000,
>   generate       = Generate,
>   analyse        = Analyse,
>   summarise      = Summarise,
>   parallel       = TRUE,
>   store_results  = TRUE,
>   save           = TRUE,
>   max_errors     = 1000L,
>   ncores         = 15,
>   seed           = global_seeds,
>   save_details   = list(tmpfilename = "tmp_uSDT_validation_simres.qs2",
>                         out_rootdir = "Results/Simulation studies/Raw/Validation study"),
>   control        = list(store_Random.seeds = TRUE, allow_na = TRUE,
>                         allow_nan = TRUE),
>   packages       = c("uSDT", "lme4"),
>   filename       = "uSDT_validation_simres.rds"
> )

Output shown here is capped at the last 5000 lines per stream to keep the report readable. The complete, untruncated output of every script is stored in the module result: reproducibility_check_output$run_results$stdout (and $stderr), one row per script.

Dependencies were installed into a throwaway library before running: 26 succeeded, 0 failed. afex, dplyr, effectsize, emmeans, ggplot2, gridExtra, haven, httr, kableExtra, knitr, lme4, logspline, metafor, minqa, numDeriv, osfr, patchwork, psychmeta, R.matlab, remotes, scales, SimDesign, tibble, tidyr, tidyverse, uSDT were installed.

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

9 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). They were only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: 1. greenwald2017_prepare_data.R at uSDT_pub_zenodo.zip/R scripts/Empirical illustrations/1. greenwald2017_prepare_data.R (same as 1. greenwald2017_prepare_data.R at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RicardoReySaez/uSDT_pub/main/R%20scripts/Empirical%20illustrations/1.%20greenwald2017_prepare_data.R); Reported vs. reproduced

16 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 1 matched (1 fully, 0 partially) — 6.2% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

SPSS data without syntax

An SPSS data file (.sav/.por) is present but no SPSS syntax file (.sps) was found, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in jamovi (.omv) or JASP (.jasp) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

MATLAB code, no reproducible output

16 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run diary('output.txt') (or diary on) before the analysis and diary off after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use publish('script.m', 'pdf') (or the Live Editor’s Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.
