However, when sensitivities are estimated from a finite number of trials using the conventional two-step approach, measurement error distorts both correlations and regression intercepts. With 80 trials per task (reliability ≈ .70, a value sometimes considered acceptable in the psychometric literature; Nunnally, 1978), the population correlation decreases to .54 and the intercept increases to .10 (Figure 3B). With only 20 trials (reliability ≈ .35), the correlation drops to .27 and the intercept increases to .22 (Figure 3C). Crucially, for the same 40 participants, the intercept becomes significantly positive with both 80 trials (0.22, 95% CI [0.03, 0.40]; Figure 3E) and 20 trials (0.29, 95% CI [0.05, 0.53]; Figure 3F), incorrectly suggesting that influence persists in the absence of awareness. Note that these biases cannot be simply fixed by collecting larger sample sizes; with few trials, having more participants would only dangerously increase the confidence in biased estimations. 7.

Finally, as illustrated above, the correlation hypothesis faces the same inferential challenge discussed earlier for simple dissociations. A nonsignificant correlation does not establish the genuine absence of a relationship between influence and awareness. Instead, researchers need methods that both address the impact of measurement error and can distinguish evidence for a null or negligible correlation from inconclusive results, such as Bayesian hypothesis testing (Dienes, 2014; Wagenmakers, 2007) or equivalence testing (Lakens, 2017).

Addressing All Challenges in a Single Approach

Several solutions have been proposed within both frequentist (e.g., Fuller, 1987; Hunter & Schmidt, 2015; Klauer et al., 1998; Lublinsky et al., 2026; Meyen et al., 2022; Spearman, 1904) and Bayesian (e.g., Dienes, 2014; Goldstein et al., 2022; Malejka et al., 2021; Matzke et al., 2017; Rouder & Haaf, 2019) frameworks, but they typically address only one of these limitations in isolation. Applied researchers are therefore left with a patchwork of complex techniques that differ in their assumptions, require advanced modeling knowledge, and often lack accessible software implementations.

In this article, we propose a single-step approach to address these challenges, based on a multilevel extension of SDT (DeCarlo, 2010). The {uSDT} package integrates the necessary procedures into a single function call, allowing researchers to test the unconscious processing 7 Meanwhile, the estimated group-level dissociation, not shown in the figure, was significantly negative with infinite trials (-0.16, 95% CI [-0.26, -0.05]), but became nonsignificant with both 80 trials (-0.08, 95% CI [-0.25, 0.09]) and 20 trials (-0.12, 95% CI [-0.41, 0.16]), despite the awareness task being more sensitive in the underlying population.

hypotheses while addressing the common challenges: First, researchers' measures of influence and awareness can be expressed on a common sensitivity scale (𝑑 ′ ), using the approach of Meyen et al. (2022) when necessary. Second, by jointly modeling trial-level responses, the model accounts for measurement error and different numbers of trials across tasks, allowing researchers to estimate the differences and relationships between their true sensitivities. Third, the {uSDT} package supports both Bayesian hypothesis testing and frequentist equivalence testing, allowing researchers to evaluate evidence for null or negligible effects rather than relying on nonsignificant results. Furthermore, unlike previous solutions to the problems outlined above, this framework requires minimal familiarity with linear mixed modeling, which is already very popular and well-known for most experimental psychologists

Comparing the Sensitivity of Influence and Awareness Tasks

As discussed in the Introduction, the group-level dissociation hypothesis concerns whether the influence task is more sensitive to the relevant information than the awareness task. A meaningful comparison therefore requires two things: expressing sensitivity in both tasks on a common scale and collecting enough information from each task to achieve adequate statistical power to detect a difference between them.

We already explained why comparing the sensitivities of influence and awareness tasks requires both measures to be expressed on a common SDT scale (𝑑 ′ ). When tasks involve binary discrimination responses-such as identifying whether a stimulus was present or absent-, sensitivity can be estimated directly from the trial-level responses using SDT. However, when performance is measured using response times (RTs), an additional step is necessary because differences in mean RTs do not directly quantify sensitivity.

To overcome this challenge, we use the approach proposed by Meyen et al. (2022), which allows us to convert RTs into a measure of sensitivity similar to that of the awareness task.

Specifically, each participant's median RT 8 is used as a threshold to classify trials according to 8 The median classifier is optimal when RT distributions are normal or lognormal with a common dispersion parameter and different location parameters across conditions, and both conditions have equal numbers of trials (see Meyen et al., 2022, Supplemental Materials B). Note, however, that using the median as the classification threshold their experimental condition. For example, in a priming task where congruent trials are expected to produce faster responses, RTs below the median (i.e., fast responses) are classified as "congruent" and those above it (i.e., slow responses) as "incongruent". Comparing these classifications with the actual experimental conditions quantifies the kind of classifications that participants are asked to perform in typical awareness tasks, and provides the binary responses needed for any conventional SDT analysis. Under the appropriate assumptions, this procedure allows influence and awareness sensitivities to be estimated on the same scale. Our multilevel model then jointly analyzes these trial-level classifications, estimating the sensitivities and their relationships.

Accounting for Measurement Error to Estimate True Sensitivities

Even when both tasks are expressed on the same sensitivity scale, individual sensitivity estimates remain subject to measurement error. Imagine using a scale to compare the weights of two objects. If each object is weighed only once, the observed difference may reflect their actual weights, random fluctuations in the measurements, or both. By weighing each object repeatedly, we can see how much the readings vary even when the underlying weight remains unchanged. The same principle applies to experimental tasks: observed differences between participants may reflect genuine differences in sensitivity, random variation across trials, or both. By modeling individual trial responses, multilevel models can account for this latter source of variability when estimating individual sensitivities and how they vary across participants (Haines et al., 2025; Rouder & Haaf, 2019).

To understand this distinction, consider that each participant has an underlying sensitivity in both the influence (𝐼) and awareness (𝐴) tasks, denoted by 𝑑 ′ 𝑖𝐼 and 𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝐴 , respectively, for participant 𝑖. As illustrated in Figure 3, these true sensitivities represent the values that would be obtained from an infinite number of trials, eliminating trial noise. Across participants, these sensitivities may differ in their average values, their variability, and the extent to which they are implicitly fixes the response criterion to zero in the influence task. This restriction can be relaxed by data-driven approaches that estimate the optimal classification threshold from training data and evaluate its performance on held-out trials (Franz & von Luxburg, 2015). related. We can characterize these differences using five population parameters: two mean sensitivities (𝜇 𝐼 and 𝜇 𝐴 ), two between-participant standard deviations (𝜎 𝐼 and 𝜎 𝐴 ), and their correlation (𝜌). Assuming a bivariate normal distribution, as is common in hierarchical models (DeCarlo, 2010; Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002; Rouder & Haaf, 2019), these parameters can be expressed as follows:

These five parameters contain all the information needed to evaluate our three hypotheses.

The group-level dissociation hypothesis concerns the difference in mean sensitivity between tasks (𝜇 𝐼 -𝜇 𝐴 ), the correlation hypothesis concerns the association between true sensitivities (𝜌), and the intercept hypothesis concerns the expected influence sensitivity when awareness sensitivity is zero. Under the assumed bivariate normal distribution, this last quantity corresponds to the regression intercept (𝛽 0 ) of true influence sensitivity on true awareness sensitivity:

By estimating these population parameters directly from trial-level responses, the multilevel SDT model allows researchers to evaluate all three hypotheses while accounting for measurement error. It also accommodates differing numbers of trials across tasks and participants, and allows researchers to quantify the reliability of their measures. In the next section, we introduce the multilevel SDT model used to estimate these parameters directly from trial-level responses.

A Multilevel Signal Detection Theory Model

Multilevel models (also known as hierarchical or mixed-effects models, Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002) are already familiar in experimental psychology, in part due to accessible tutorials and practical guidelines written for experimental psychologists (Baayen et al., 2008; Barr et al., 2013; Brysbaert & Debeer, 2025; Hoffman & Rovine, 2007; Meteyard & Davies, 2020; Singmann & Kellen, 2020). Their main advantage is that they naturally accommodate the hierarchical structure of experimental data: trial responses (level 1) nested within participants (level 2).

Within this framework, trial-to-trial variability within participants (i.e., measurement error) is modeled separately from variability in participant-specific parameters (i.e., true individual differences). In this sense, multilevel models can be conceptualized as psychometric models in experimental psychology, and have been used to estimate correlations corrected for measurement error across tasks (Rouder et al., 2023; Rouder & Haaf, 2019), as well as test-retest reliability (Haines et al., 2025; Rouder & Haaf, 2019). Building on this foundation, we introduce a multilevel SDT model that jointly analyzes trial-level responses from the awareness and influence tasks. We begin by assuming that both tasks are expressed on a common sensitivity scale, either directly or by applying the transformation proposed by Meyen et al. (2022) to the influence measure, where all responses, either discrete or continuous (such as RTs), will be transformed first into "classifications" following the standard logic of SDT.

Model Formulation

Let 𝑦 𝑖 𝑗ℓ denote the observed response of participant 𝑖 in task 𝑗 on trial ℓ, coded as 1 for one response category and 0 for the other. For example, in a typical priming experiment, participants' RTs may be used to classify trials as congruent (1) or incongruent (0), or displays as repeated (1) or new (0) in the case of a contextual cuing experiment, as we illustrate below. We assume that each response follows a Bernoulli distribution: where 𝜋 𝑖 𝑗ℓ is the probability of a response coded as 1 on that trial.

This probability is modeled using a probit regression: where Φ -1 is the inverse standard normal cumulative distribution function (i.e., the "probit" link function), 𝑥 𝑖 𝑗ℓ represents the experimental condition (coded as 0.5 for signal trials and -0.5 for noise trials), and 𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝑗 and 𝑐 𝑖 𝑗 are the participant-and task-specific sensitivity and response criterion, respectively.

We further assume that these participant-and task-specific parameters jointly follow a multivariate normal distribution: (

Here, 𝒅 ′ 𝑖 = (𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝐴 , 𝑑 ′ 𝑖𝐼 ) ⊤ contains participant 𝑖's sensitivities in the awareness (𝐴) and influence (𝐼) tasks, while 𝒄 𝑖 = (𝑐 𝑖 𝐴 , 𝑐 𝑖𝐼 ) ⊤ contains the corresponding response criteria. The vectors 𝝁 𝑑 ′ and 𝝁 𝑐 contain the population means of these parameters, known as fixed effects in multilevel terminology. Individual participants can deviate from these means, and these deviations are the random effects. The matrix 𝚺 describes how much these random effects vary across participants and how they covary. Its upper-left block, 𝚺 𝑑 ′ , contains the variances of true sensitivities and their covariance across tasks, while 𝚺 𝑐 describes the corresponding variances and covariance of response criteria. Finally, the off-diagonal blocks, 𝚺 𝑑 ′ 𝑐 = 𝚺 ⊤ 𝑐𝑑 ′ , describe how sensitivities and response criteria covary, both within and across tasks.

Notice that 𝝁 𝑑 ′ and 𝚺 𝑑 ′ are exactly the mean vector and covariance matrix of true sensitivities introduced in Equation 1. This means that the five population parameters defining our three hypotheses are estimated directly by the multilevel SDT model itself. Because these parameters are estimated jointly from trial-level responses, the model accounts for measurement error without requiring separate estimates of individual sensitivities or their reliability. All three hypotheses can therefore be tested using the model's parameters, avoiding the distortions introduced by the conventional two-step approach.

Participant-Specific Sensitivities

As shown in Equation 4, the participant-specific sensitivities, 𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝑗 , are themselves parameters of the multilevel model. As discussed earlier, these parameters can be understood as true sensitivities, in the sense that they represent the values that would be recovered from infinite trials, assuming the model is correctly specified. However, this does not mean that the model can recover these values perfectly from a finite number of trials.

Consider a participant whose observed sensitivity is unusually high after completing only a few trials, so this estimate is highly uncertain. Multilevel models address this uncertainty by estimating individual sensitivities using both the participant's responses and the information shared with the rest of the group, represented by the multivariate normal distribution in Equation 5. The resulting estimates represent a compromise between these two sources of information: the less reliable a participant's observed sensitivity, the more their estimated sensitivity is pulled toward the group mean. Figure 4 shows the estimates of the multilevel model for the two samples discussed in the section "Challenges for the Correlation and Intercept Hypotheses", in which each participant completed 80 (Panel A) or 20 (Panel B) trials per task. This mechanism, known as partial pooling or shrinkage (James & Stein, 1961), is particularly useful from a psychometric perspective because random measurement error does not systematically affect the group mean. In fact, this same principle is captured by a century-old psychometric equation for estimating true scores: Kelley's regression formula (Kelley, 1927, p. 178), where 𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝑗 is the observed sensitivity of participant 𝑖 in task 𝑗, 𝑅 𝑗 is the reliability of that task, and 𝜇 𝑗 is its population mean sensitivity (𝜇 𝐼 or 𝜇 𝐴 in Equation 1).

When reliability is perfect (𝑅 𝑗 = 1), the estimate equals the observed sensitivity. When reliability is zero (𝑅 𝑗 = 0), the observed score provides no information about individual differences, and the best estimate is the group mean.

When reliability falls between 0 and 1, Kelley's formula produces precisely the partial pooling described above. Multilevel models build on this same idea, but extend it to multiple variables that may be correlated with one another (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002).

As model-based sensitivities are estimates of true participants' sensitivities, it may be tempting to use them in subsequent analyses, such as correlations or regressions. However, Note. The samples of 40 participants with 80 (Panel A) and 20 (Panel B) trials per task from the section Challenges for the Correlation and Intercept Hypotheses, reanalyzed using the multilevel SDT model. Gray points show observed sensitivities from the two-step approach; black points show multilevel estimates, with segments connecting each participant's scores. Solid lines show the model-implied regressions of influence on awareness sensitivity; dashed lines show the true population regression. Open circles indicate estimated intercepts (95% CIs). Upper-right values report the estimated intercept and correlation between true sensitivities ( ρ), both with 95% CIs.

accurately estimating each participant's true sensitivity is not the same as accurately estimating how sensitivities vary and relate to one another across participants. To improve these predictions, partial pooling exploits the classical bias-variance tradeoff (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017), introducing some bias toward the population mean in exchange for reduced estimation variance (Efron & Morris, 1975; James & Stein, 1961). A perhaps surprising consequence is that, if we calculated the sample variance of these individual estimates, we would generally obtain a smaller value than the corresponding variance in Equation 5 estimated by the multilevel model (Louis, 1984; Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh, 2004). The same applies to covariances, which will generally differ from those estimated in 𝚺 𝑑 ′ . Although both sets of quantities may appear to describe the same individual differences, the former describe the variability of individual predictions, whereas the latter describe the variability of true sensitivities in the population. Correlations and regression coefficients calculated from these predictions can therefore yield biased estimates of population relationships (Devlieger et al., 2016; Skrondal & Laake, 2001). 9 For population-level inference, we should instead use the parameters estimated directly by the multilevel model. The correlation between true sensitivities can be obtained from 𝚺 𝑑 ′ , while the regression intercept can be calculated from the population parameters, as shown in Equation 2.

Other individual-difference questions can often be addressed by extending the model to include additional covariates or outcomes, allowing the relationships of interest to be estimated while accounting for measurement error.

However, accounting for measurement error does not eliminate uncertainty when few trials are available. Even when both tasks are expressed on a common sensitivity scale, differences in the number of trials can still affect statistical power. As illustrated in Figure 5, collecting too few trials in one of the tasks can make genuine differences in sensitivity between tasks difficult to detect (and the multilevel SDT model cannot fix this, as we say in Spain: "Where there's no sprout, there's no spud."). Thus, a meaningful sensitivity comparison requires not only comparable measures, but also sufficient information from both tasks. To address this limitation, the {uSDT} package also allows researchers to evaluate statistical power when planning the sample and trial size of their experiments.

Bayesian Extension

The multilevel SDT model described above can also be estimated within a Bayesian framework (Gelman et al., 2013; Kruschke, 2015; McElreath, 2020; for hierarchical Bayesian 9 Consider a simplified example in which true awareness-and influence-task sensitivities have a correlation of 𝜌 = .50 and SDs of 𝜎 𝐴 = 1 and 𝜎 𝐼 = 2, giving a population regression slope of 𝛽 = 𝜌 • 𝜎 𝐼 /𝜎 𝐴 = 1. Suppose awareness-task sensitivity is measured with perfect reliability, so its true scores can be obtained directly. Influence-task sensitivity, however, has a reliability of .64 and must be estimated. If we predict these sensitivities using univariate shrinkage, as illustrated by Kelley's formula (Equation 6), the resulting predictions have an SD of 1.6 and a correlation of .40 with awareness-task sensitivity. Regressing these predictions on awareness-task sensitivity gives a slope of 0.64 instead of 1. In our joint multilevel model, shrinkage also uses information from correlated parameters, making its consequences for regression slopes more complex.

The open circle marks the minimum number of awareness-task trials required to reach 80% power (dotted line) SDT models, see Rouder & Lu, 2005; Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013). This extension is relatively straightforward and is already implemented in the {uSDT} package: the model structure remains unchanged, but prior distributions are assigned to its parameters. Combining these priors with the observed trial-level likelihood yields posterior distributions for all model parameters, including the five population parameters defining our three hypotheses. These posterior distributions can be used to compute credible intervals and, with appropriate prior specifications, Bayes factors to quantify evidence for or against the null hypotheses (Dienes, 2014; Wagenmakers, 2007).

One important consideration is that specifying priors on the five population parameters in Equation 1 also implicitly defines a prior on the regression intercept in Equation 2, since the intercept is a function of these parameters. This induced prior may not reflect the researcher's prior expectations when testing the intercept hypothesis using Bayes factors. When previous empirical evidence informs the priors on these population parameters, researchers can inspect the resulting prior on the intercept through prior predictive checking (Gelman et al., 2020) to assess its plausibility. Alternatively, the model can be parameterized as a latent regression (with the argument latent = "regression" in the hsdt() function), allowing a prior to be specified directly on its intercept. In this parameterization, the intercept replaces the influence-task mean sensitivity (𝜇 𝐼 ), while the remaining four population parameters keep their own priors. The influence-task mean is no longer sampled directly, but is derived at each posterior draw by solving Equation 2 for 𝜇 𝐼 . As a result, both the intercept and the correlation between sensitivities (𝜌) have priors chosen by the researcher, whereas the prior on the group-level difference (𝜇 𝐼 -𝜇 𝐴 ) is induced by the others.

The Bayesian framework also allows us to consider a more flexible version of the model that relaxes the equal-variance assumption of SDT (with the argument unequal_variances = TRUE in the hsdt() function). The model presented in Equation 4 assumes that the underlying signal and noise distributions have the same variance. Relaxing this assumption introduces an additional parameter that cannot be identified from binary responses without further assumptions. However, Lages (2024) showed that this limitation can be overcome using a Bayesian hierarchical model that exploits variability in hit and false-alarm rates across participants. Assuming that sensitivity and response criterion are independent at the population level (i.e., 𝚺 𝑑𝑐 = 0), and that the relative variances of the signal and noise distributions are approximately constant across participants, the ratio of the variances of their z-transformed false-alarm and hit rates can be used to estimate the relative variances of the underlying signal and noise distributions.

Model Assumptions

The multilevel SDT model makes several assumptions about how responses are generated and how sensitivities vary across participants. At the trial level, it assumes normally distributed evidence with equal variances across stimulus conditions, although our Bayesian extension relaxes the equal-variance assumption. It also requires that performance in both tasks can be expressed on a common sensitivity scale. For tasks based on RTs, this involves converting continuous responses into binary outcomes, and the choice of conversion may affect the results. At the participant level, sensitivities and response criteria are assumed to follow a single multivariate normal distribution. This last assumption deserves particular attention. A single normal distribution represents individual differences as continuous variation within one population. However, some theories propose that aware and unaware participants constitute qualitatively distinct populations (Goldstein et al., 2022; Lublinsky et al., 2026). Such an alternative could be accommodated within our framework using a mixture SDT model (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013), but would require additional assumptions about how these populations are defined. For example, should the unaware population include only participants with exactly zero awareness-task sensitivity, or also those with sensitivity below a specified threshold? Furthermore, assigning participants to these populations would be uncertain when sensitivity is measured imperfectly. Although mixture models can account for this uncertainty without requiring definitive classifications, they cannot determine what constitutes unawareness.

But suppose that aware and unaware participants do constitute distinct populations. We would still be interested in the relationship between awareness and influence, particularly their correlation and regression intercept. Can our multilevel SDT model accurately recover these parameters when the true population consists of distinct aware and unaware subpopulations, despite assuming a single multivariate normal distribution? Simulation Study 2, presented in the next section, was specifically designed to address this question.

Simulation Studies

We conducted two simulation studies to evaluate the multilevel SDT model before applying it to empirical data. Simulation Study 1 was a validation study in which data were generated from our model to assess parameter recovery and the validity of inferences on all three hypotheses across a broad range of conditions. Simulation Study 2 was a robustness study examining whether inferences on the correlation and intercept remained valid when true sensitivities were generated from the alternative population models of Klauer et al. (1998) and Goldstein et al. (2022). Both approaches were developed to estimate the relationship between awareness and influence measures while accounting for measurement error, but unlike our model both assume two subpopulations of participants: those with no awareness (𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝐴 = 0) and those with positive awareness-task sensitivity. Although they formalize these subpopulations differently, neither population model follows the bivariate normal distribution assumed by our model. Here, we summarize the simulation designs and main results, with full methodological details provided in the Supplemental Material.

Method

Design

In Simulation Study 1, true sensitivities were drawn from the bivariate normal distribution in Equation 1, and trial responses were generated from Equation 4. We manipulated five factors: sample size (𝑁), trials per condition (𝐾), reliability (𝑅), correlation between true sensitivities (𝜌), and regression intercept (𝛽 0 ). To manipulate reliability for a given number of trials, we derived the variances of true sensitivities from the target reliability (𝑅) and the sampling variance of 𝑑 ′ with 𝐾 trials per condition (Gourevitch & Galanter, 1967; see the Supplemental Material).

In Simulation Study 2, true sensitivities were generated from the population models of Klauer et al. (1998) and Goldstein et al. (2022). We manipulated six factors: generating model, 𝑁, 𝐾, proportion of unaware participants (𝜋 0 ), correlation (𝜌), and intercept (𝛽 0 ). Unlike in Study 1, reliability was not manipulated directly but depended on 𝐾 and, for the awareness task, 𝜋 0.

Influence-task reliabilities were .22, .46, and .58 for 𝐾 = 10, 30, and 50, respectively, comparable to 𝑅 = .2, .5, and .6 in Study 1. Awareness-task reliability was higher (.48 to .93) due to greater variability in true sensitivities (Table S9 of the Supplemental Material). Crossing all factor levels (Table 1) yielded 1,260 and 648 conditions in Studies 1 and 2, respectively, with 1,000 simulated datasets per condition.

Procedure

Both studies were conducted in R version 4.5.0 (R Core Team, 2024), using {SimDesign} (Chalmers & Adkins, 2020) to manage the simulation workflow. Each dataset was analyzed with

Note.

In Study 1, 𝜇 𝐴 = 0.2, and true-sensitivity SDs were derived from 𝑅 and 𝐾. In Study 2, 𝜎 𝐼 = 0.3, and 𝜌 and 𝛽 0 refer to regressions on awareness-task 𝑑 ′ (Klauer) or chance-centered accuracy (Goldstein). In both studies, awareness-task criteria varied (SD = 0.3), and the influencetask criterion was fixed at 0.

the frequentist multilevel SDT model implemented in {uSDT} (Rey-Sáez, Garre-Frutos, et al., 2026), fitted by maximum likelihood using {lme4} (Bates et al., 2015). We used 95% Wald CIs (computed on the log scale for SDs) and the three hypothesis tests implemented in {uSDT}. Fits with singular random-effects covariance matrices (e.g., an SD estimated at zero or a correlation at ±1) were classified as untestable for H2 and H3 because SEs for the correlation and intercept were unavailable.

Analysis

For each parameter, we computed bias (mean estimate minus true value) and empirical coverage of the 95% CIs. For each hypothesis, we computed the rejection rate at the .05 level, representing Type I error when the null hypothesis was true and statistical power otherwise. The intercept was evaluated only in testable fits, as its estimate becomes unstable when 𝜎 𝐴 approaches zero (Equation 2). All other parameters were evaluated in every fit, and the proportion of untestable fits was reported separately. To summarize parameter recovery across conditions, we computed Lin's (1989) concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) between the mean estimates and true values, which measures agreement with the identity line. Following Bradley's (1978) liberal criterion, acceptable coverage and Type I error rates were [.925, .975] and [.025, .075], respectively. Results for individual conditions and ANOVA metamodels examining the effects of the simulation factors (Skrondal, 2000) are reported in the Supplemental Material.

Results

Simulation Study 1: Validation

All but 106 of the 1,260,000 fits converged (0.008% returned estimation errors). Figure 6 shows the recovery of the population parameters. The influence-task mean sensitivity, group-level dissociation (H1), and SDs were recovered almost perfectly (CCC ≥ .995), and the awareness-task mean sensitivity, fixed at 0.2, showed biases below .015 in every condition (Table S2 in the Supplemental Material). Recovery was also strong for the correlation (H2; CCC = .955) and intercept (H3; CCC = .952), although their estimates were less accurate, particularly under low reliability. Note. Each point represents a simulation condition, averaged over 1,000 replications. Colors indicate reliability values. Dashed lines indicate perfect recovery. CCC = concordance correlation coefficient. The awareness-task mean (fixed at 0.2) is omitted, and the intercept was computed over testable fits.

As shown in Table 2, the group-level dissociation was recovered almost perfectly at every level of reliability, whereas recovery of the correlation and intercept was poor at 𝑅 = .1 (CCC = .72 and .79, respectively), but improved substantially at 𝑅 = .3 (CCC ≥ .98). Low reliability also increased the frequency of boundary estimates (SDs of zero or correlations of ±1), leaving fits untestable for H2 and H3 (Table 3). At 𝑅 = .1, 71% of fits were untestable, ranging from 56% at 𝑁 = 200 to 83% at 𝑁 = 30, compared with less than 9% at 𝑅 ≥ .5. Moreover, at extremely low reliability, correlations were biased toward zero when their true values were high (bias = -.31 at 𝑅 = .1 and 𝜌 = .8), whereas with 𝑅 ≥ .3 they were slightly overestimated on average (by at most .09 in any condition). The intercept, in turn, was overestimated when the correlation was strong and reliability extremely low (bias = .11 at 𝑅 = .1 and 𝜌 = .8 when 𝛽0 = 0, and .05 at 𝑅 = .2), because the attenuated slope inflates it. Note. Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) between true values and mean estimates across 1,000 replications, computed over 180 conditions per reliability level. The intercept was computed over testable fits. See Figure S2 for scatterplots.

Coverage and rejection rates are summarized in Table 3. Inferences on H1 were valid at every level of reliability: the coverage of 𝜇 𝐼 -𝜇 𝐴 ranged from .917 to .970 and met Bradley's criterion in 99% of conditions. For H2 and H3, results differed between low (𝑅 ≤ .3) and moderate to high reliability (𝑅 ≥ .4). With 𝑅 ≤ .3, 48% of fits were untestable on average (up to 86%), leaving only a selected subset for inference. In this subset, CIs for H2 were conservative in most conditions, but with 𝜌 = .8 their coverage fell below .925 in 68% of the conditions, down to .85. Type I error for H2 was below .025 in 75% of null conditions. Type I error for H3 met Bradley's criterion in only 46% of null conditions: it was conservative in 49% and exceeded .075 in 9 (maximum = .11), all with 𝑅 ≤ .2 and 𝜌 = .8, where the intercept was overestimated. With 𝑅 ≥ .4, only 8% of fits were untestable, Type I error for H2 never exceeded .067, and Type I error for H3 met Bradley's criterion in 98% of null conditions (maximum = .073). The power of H1 increased with effect size, sample size, and number of trials, as expected for a test of a group-level mean (Figure S6 in the Supplemental Material). We therefore focus on H2 and H3, whose power depended more directly on reliability (Figure 7). Untestable fits were counted as non-rejections, reflecting the power researchers can expect in practice. Considering only testable fits yielded higher power when boundary estimates were frequent (up to .36 higher;

Figure S8), but these constituted a selected subset of fits. With 𝑅 ≤ .3, power for H2 never reached .80, even with 𝑁 = 200 (maximum = .61), and H3 reached .80 only for 𝛽0 = .30, 𝑅 = .3, and 𝑁 = 200. With 𝑁 = 200 and 𝑅 ≥ .5, power was at least .82 for correlations of .4 or larger and .98 for 𝛽0 = .30. Small correlations were difficult to detect: power for 𝜌 = .2 never exceeded .50.

Power for 𝛽0 = .15 leveled off at .79 to .82 with 𝑁 = 200 and 𝑅 ≥ .5, because 𝛽 0 was fixed while 𝜎 𝐼 increased with 𝑅, so the same intercept was a smaller effect relative to individual differences.

Overall, the multilevel SDT model showed good parameter recovery and generally well-calibrated inferences across the simulated conditions. As expected, low reliability made the Note. Proportion of the 1,000 replications per condition in which H2 or H3 was rejected (𝛼 = .05).

Simulation Study 2: Robustness

Only 31 of the 648,000 fits returned estimation errors. Boundary fits were less frequent than in Study 1, because the awareness measure was more reliable, occurring in 8% and 6% of fits under the models of Klauer et al. (1998) and Goldstein et al. (2022), respectively, mostly with 𝐾 = 10, when the influence measure was least reliable, and small samples. Under both generating models, the correlation and intercept were recovered accurately (all CCCs ≥ .991). Coverage was close to .95 for the intercept and conservative for the correlation with few trials, approaching .95 as the number of trials, and thus the reliability of the influence task, increased (from .981 and .976 with 𝐾 = 10 to .951 and .956 with 𝐾 = 50). Type I error rates remained close to the nominal level, never exceeding .080 (Table 4). Under the model of Klauer et al. (1998), the multilevel SDT model accurately recovered both the population correlation and intercept, despite the violation of its assumed bivariate normal distribution, and even though up to 80% of participants had a true awareness-task sensitivity of exactly zero. Both parameters were also accurately recovered under Goldstein et al. (2022), although a complication arises in interpreting the intercept. Goldstein et al. define the regression of influence-task sensitivity on awareness accuracy, rather than 𝑑 ′ . This means that the regression is estimating an intercept closely related to that of Goldstein, but not exactly the same. When awareness and the influence effect are related, our intercept is slightly larger than the one manipulated in their model, even when the latter is zero. In our simulations, the difference was at most 0.045, and when the manipulated intercept was zero, H3 was rejected in up to 15% of the replications, with rejection rates above .075 in 13% of these conditions. The difference comes from participants with almost perfect accuracy, which the model of Goldstein et al. allows. If the accuracy of aware participants did not exceed .75 (i.e., a 𝑑 ′ of 1.35), the intercept defined by Goldstein et al. and the intercept estimated by our model would differ by at most 0.004. The Supplemental Material reports these results in detail and explains where the difference comes from (Tables S10-S14 and Figures S9-S11).

The multilevel SDT model thus provided generally robust inferences under both generating models, even when the intercept defined by Goldstein et al. (2022) did not exactly correspond to the one estimated by our model. This makes it a promising approach even when the population consists of distinct subpopulations of aware and unaware participants.

Empirical Illustrations

We now illustrate how the multilevel SDT model can be applied to empirical data and compare its conclusions with those obtained using conventional analyses. We fit the models with Masked Conditioning Greenwald and De Houwer (2017) conducted 20 experiments investigating whether conditioning can occur without conscious awareness, including 14 experiments with masked conditioned stimuli (CSs) and 6 with visible CSs. Across experiments, participants categorized either words as "pleasant" or "unpleasant", or first names as "male" or "female". During acquisition, each word or name (unconditioned stimulus, US) was preceded by one of two four-consonant strings (CSs; e.g., "NPLW" or "DHJF"), each consistently paired with one US category (e.g., "NPLW" with pleasant words and "DHJF" with unpleasant words). In the subsequent conditioning test (influence task), CS-US pairings were randomized and conditioning was measured as 𝑑 ′ (e.g., a "pleasant" response counted as a hit when preceded by "NPLW" and as a false alarm when preceded by "DHJF", regardless of whether the word itself was pleasant or unpleasant). In the masked-CS experiments, a subsequent visibility test (awareness task) required participants to identify which of the two consonant strings had appeared on each trial, measuring awareness with 𝑑 ′ as well. The data are publicly available at https://osf.io/ydeza.

For our illustration, we use Experiment 1c (S18), the last and largest of their 14 unconscious conditioning experiments. CSs were presented for 75 ms following a forward mask, and a response window (333-467 ms after US onset) encouraged rapid categorization. Of 386 participants, 350 met the authors' inclusion criteria and completed 192 acquisition trials, 96 conditioning test trials, and 144 visibility test trials. The authors regressed conditioning on visibility, interpreting a positive intercept as evidence of conditioning at zero visibility. To account for measurement error in the visibility measure, they also applied the errors-in-variables correction of Klauer et al. (1998), after which the intercept remained statistically significant. The Klauer regression yielded a positive intercept, 0.10, 95% CI [0.08, 0.13], and a slope close to zero.

Together with the finding that no participant showed perfect awareness of the CS-US contingency, the authors interpreted these results as evidence of unconscious conditioning.

We fitted the multilevel SDT model to the trial-level data from Experiment 1c (S18), applying the original authors' exclusion criteria. 10 We estimated the model using both frequentist and Bayesian methods. Because the authors' conclusion rests on the regression intercept, the Bayesian model used the latent regression parameterization, with a weakly informative prior placed directly on its intercept, N (0, 1), a uniform prior on the correlation, and the default priors of {uSDT} on the remaining parameters (see Appendix A). For comparison, we also applied the errors-in-variables correction of Klauer et al. (1998), implemented in {uSDT}, to the 𝑑 ′ scores 10 Although we focus on Experiment 1c (S18) here, we also prepared the trial-level data and fitted the same models to the other 17 datasets from Series 1 of Greenwald and De Houwer (2017). The code for reproducing these analyses is available in the R scripts/Extra analysis folder of the project repositories.

The awareness task was substantially more sensitive to the CS than the influence task (mean 𝑑 ′ = 0.62 vs. 0.09, corresponding to approximately 62% vs. 52% correct classification of individual trials; BF10 = 7.8 × 10 8 ). The group-level analysis therefore showed the opposite of the expected dissociation. This difference is illustrated in Figure 8, which shows the population ROC curves for the awareness and influence tasks. Evidence concerning the correlation between true task sensitivities was inconclusive (𝜌 = -.24, 95% CrI [-.96, .84]; BF01 = 1.13). In contrast, the latent intercept provided extreme evidence for conditioning at zero visibility (𝑑 ′ = 0.10, 95% CrI [0.07, 0.13]; BF10 = 97,738), consistent with the original analyses and the correction of Klauer et al. (1998).

These results must be interpreted in light of the extremely low reliability of the influence measure (reliability = .01, 95% CrI [.00, .05], compared with .94, 95% CrI [.93, .95] for the awareness measure). As illustrated in Figure 9, although observed influence sensitivities vary considerably across participants (top panel), the multilevel model attributes nearly all this variability to measurement error, shrinking individual estimates toward the group mean (bottom panel). The estimated between-participant variance in true influence-task sensitivity was so close to zero that we could not obtain standard errors for the other hypotheses from the frequentist Note. model. With virtually no true variability in conditioning, its relationship with CS visibility is difficult to evaluate, explaining why the correlation between true sensitivities could not be reliably estimated. Under these circumstances, the regression slope approaches zero (-0.01) regardless of the true correlation, and the intercept becomes nearly identical to the mean conditioning effect.

Although this produces strong evidence for a positive intercept, interpreting it as evidence of conditioning without conscious awareness is problematic, because the data cannot establish either the presence or the absence of an association between conditioning and awareness.

Contextual Cuing of Visual Attention

Vadillo et al. (2025) investigated how to improve the reliability of contextual-cuing measures by manipulating several experimental features (set size, color vs. grayscale, and distractor-target similarity) and conducting a multiverse analysis of different preprocessing Note. Gray circles show observed participant-level sensitivities, and green points show posterior mean estimates from the multilevel SDT model. Connecting segments illustrate shrinkage. Lines represent the observed regression (top) and the model-implied latent regression (bottom), with 95% confidence and credible bands, respectively. Open circles mark the intercepts. b₀ = intercept; b₁ = slope. P-values in the bottom panel are two-sided posterior p-values. Figure generated using the {uSDT} R package. showed greater sensitivity in the recognition than in the search task, but no significant correlation between observed sensitivities (𝑟 = .10, 95% CI [-.10, .29]) and a significantly positive regression intercept (0.10, 95% CI [0.06, 0.14]), the two latter typically interpreted as evidence of contextual cuing without awareness.

The multilevel SDT model supported only the first of these conclusions. The awareness task was more sensitive than the influence task (mean 𝑑 ′ = 0.23 vs. 0.11, corresponding to approximately 55% vs. 52% correct classification of individual trials; BF10 = 6.43), again showing the opposite of the expected group-level dissociation. Evidence concerning the correlation between true sensitivities was inconclusive (𝜌 = .29, 95% CrI [-.71, .96]; BF01 = 1.20). The latent intercept was close to zero, with moderate evidence against contextual cuing at zero awareness (𝑑 ′ = 0.05, 95% CrI [-0.40, 0.46]; BF01 = 6.77).

The discrepancy with the two-step approach can be explained by the low reliability of the awareness measure. With 64 recognition trials, its reliability was .12 (95% CrI [.00, .34]), compared with the influence measure's reliability of .29 (95% CrI [.06, .48]). Much of the observed variability in recognition therefore reflected measurement error, which can attenuate the correlation and inflate the intercept when ignored (Figure 10). As in the previous example, low reliability complicates the interpretation of a positive intercept as evidence of unconscious processing.

Masked Affective Priming

Wentura et al. ( 2025) investigated whether the processing of emotional facial expressions requires awareness, revisiting the conclusions of Lähteenmäki et al. (2015). For our illustration, we use their preregistered Experiment 2a. In the influence task, a face expressing anger or sadness (the prime) was presented for 40 ms between a forward and a backward mask, followed by a visible target face that participants categorized as "angry" or "sad" as quickly as possible.

Affective priming (influence measure) was computed as the RT difference between congruent trials, in which prime and target expressed the same emotion, and incongruent trials. In the subsequent awareness task, participants categorized the emotion of the masked prime. Eighty-six participants completed 360 trials per task, equally balanced between conditions. The data are publicly available at https://osf.io/9t4pk.

The authors tested the group-level dissociation hypothesis separately for each task.

Responses were 6 ms faster on congruent than incongruent trials, with strong evidence for a priming effect (BF10 = 10.57). In contrast, mean sensitivity in the awareness task was very low, with only anecdotal evidence that it differed from zero (BF10 = 1.93). They also found no correlation between the priming effect and awareness sensitivity (𝑟 (84) = -.03, BF01 = 7.20).

The intercept hypothesis was not tested. Based on these findings, the authors concluded that masked affective priming does not require awareness.

We fitted the multilevel SDT model to the trial-level data, following the authors' preprocessing procedures, which excluded errors and RT outliers (16.1% of trials). Following Meyen et al. (2022), we dichotomized RTs at each participant's median, treating faster responses as "congruent" responses (and slower as "incongruent" responses). We considered congruent trials as signal (and incongruent trials as noise) to compute a 𝑑 ′ as the sensitivity of the influence measure. For the awareness task, sad primes were treated as signal (and angry primes as noise).

To mirror the original Bayesian analyses, we fitted only the Bayesian model, using the authors' Note. Lines represent the observed regression (top) and the model-implied latent regression (bottom), with 95% confidence and credible bands, respectively. Open circles mark the intercepts. b₀ = intercept; b₁ = slope. P-values in the bottom panel are two-sided posterior p-values. Figure generated using the {uSDT} R package.

priors for the mean task sensitivities and their correlation (see Appendix A). Bayes factors were computed using the Savage-Dickey density ratio for all three hypotheses and each task's mean sensitivity against zero. Results are presented in Table 7. Note. Original results are from Wentura et al. (2025). We calculated 95% CIs from reported effect sizes (N = 86). Original BFs used JASP with a two-sided Cauchy prior (r = sqrt(2)/2). Cohen's 𝑑 𝑧 is the mean within-participant effect divided by its SD. BF_01 > 1 favors the null.

The multilevel SDT model did not support the original conclusions. Testing each task separately reproduced the original pattern, with strong evidence that influence sensitivity was above zero (BF10 = 28.20) but only anecdotal evidence for awareness sensitivity (BF10 = 1.37).

However, both measures were practically equally sensitive (mean 𝑑 ′ = 0.05 vs. 0.06, corresponding to approximately 51% correct classification of individual trials in both tasks; BF01 = 11.40). The group-level analysis therefore provided strong evidence against a dissociation.

Evidence concerning the correlation between true sensitivities was inconclusive (𝜌 = .39, 95% CrI [-.12, .86]; BF01 = 0.91). The latent intercept was positive but close to zero, with only anecdotal evidence for affective priming at zero awareness (𝑑 ′ = 0.05, 95% CrI [0.01, 0.09]; BF10 = 2.06).

Although neither measure was as unreliable as in the previous examples, both still showed limited reliability. The reliability of the awareness task was .53 (95% CrI [.39, .66]), compared with reliability of the influence task of .30 (95% CrI [.06, .50]). The estimated correlation between true sensitivities (𝜌 = .39) was more than twice the observed correlation between participant-level estimates (𝑟 = .17), although evidence concerning the true correlation remained inconclusive. Evidence against a zero correlation remained inconclusive (BF01 = 0.91), but the posterior probability that the true correlation was positive was 93.7%, with a directional Bayes factor of 14.73 favoring a positive correlation over a negative or zero correlation (Figure 11). The original null correlation therefore cannot establish that affective priming is independent of awareness. The results were also sensitive to the choice of priors. With the wider priors used in the authors' sensitivity analysis (𝑟 = 1 and 𝑟 = √ 2), evidence for equal sensitivities increased (BF01 up to 22.44), while evidence for a positive intercept decreased (BF01 up to 0.83). Overall, the reanalysis provides no convincing evidence of unconscious affective priming. Note. The left panel shows the prior (dashed) and posterior (solid) densities of the latent correlation 𝜌, with the vertical dotted line marking the null value 𝜌 = 0. The ratio of the prior and posterior densities at this point yields the Savage-Dickey Bayes factor for the point-null hypothesis. The right panel shows the same posterior distribution for the directional hypothesis 𝜌 > 0; the shaded area represents the posterior probability that the true correlation is positive. The qualitative evidence labels (e.g., anecdotal, moderate, strong) follow the classification adapted from Jeffreys (1961) by Lee and Wagenmakers (2013).

Discussion

Research on unconscious processing has traditionally relied on three types of evidence: group-level dissociations between influence and awareness measures, their correlation across individuals, and the intercept of their regression.

These hypotheses are often tested using separate analyses that overlook methodological challenges: differences in statistical power and measurement scales, measurement error, and the failure to distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence. Together, these challenges can artificially inflate the apparent evidence for unconscious processing. Although several methods have been proposed to address each of these challenges in isolation, researchers must identify, understand, and implement the appropriate methods for each challenge, which can be highly demanding. In this work, we have introduced a multilevel SDT model that simultaneously addresses these challenges and allows all three hypotheses to be tested in a single step, using just one R function. By jointly analyzing trial-level responses from influence and awareness tasks, the model accounts for uncertainty in individual sensitivities and estimates the population parameters needed to evaluate each hypothesis. To facilitate its use in applied research, we have implemented the models in the R package {uSDT}, available on CRAN (Rey-Sáez, Garre-Frutos, et al., 2026). The package provides both frequentist and Bayesian implementations, allowing researchers to fit these models with minimal effort.

Reliability and Validity

Although multilevel models account for measurement error, they cannot compensate for too low reliability. When one or both tasks are highly unreliable (e.g., reliabilities below .30), the data may simply contain too little information to estimate the relationship between true sensitivities with sufficient precision. This problem cannot be solved by statistical modeling alone, but the multilevel SDT model can at least alert researchers to the substantial uncertainty surrounding these estimates. Nevertheless, researchers should prioritize improving task reliability through experimental design, for example, by increasing the number of trials or optimizing task procedures to obtain more precise measures of individual differences (e.g., Siegelman et al., 2017; Franco-Martínez, Rey-Sáez, et al., 2026; Vadillo et al., 2025; Whitehead et al., 2020).

Reliability alone, however, does not guarantee that our inferences are valid. For instance, even when measurement error is minimized and a proper sensitivity comparison is computed, inferences about unconscious processing still depend on whether the awareness task adequately measures conscious awareness (e.g., Giménez-Fernández et al., 2020; Franco-Martínez, Rey-Sáez, et al., 2026; Franco-Martínez, Ferrer-Mendieta, et al., 2026; Schmidt & Biafora, 2024). Beyond measurement validity, our model does not currently accommodate alternative criteria for inferring unconscious processing, such as the double-dissociation criterion proposed by Schmidt and Vorberg (2006). Nevertheless, note that the proposed framework could be readily extended to test this criterion with an appropriate experimental design, simply by framing H1 to test for an interaction. But in any case, while statistical modeling can help to mitigate methodological issues and improve inferences in unconscious processing research, these models cannot, by themselves, ensure the validity of the measures on which those inferences rely.

Relatedly, another consideration concerns how influence and awareness are assessed.

Consider, for example, a masked priming experiment in which participants respond to targets preceded by briefly presented primes. The influence of the primes can be assessed through their effects on RTs, whereas awareness can be measured either on the very same trials, by asking participants to report how clearly they perceived each prime (online), or in a separate detection or discrimination task (ofline, see Jimenez et al., 2025). In the former case, both responses may depend on correlated perceptual evidence, introducing dependencies at the trial level (DeCarlo, 2003; Rausch et al., 2021). Like other approaches that estimate the relationship between influence and awareness across participants (Klauer et al., 1998; Goldstein et al., 2022.), our model does not explicitly account for these dependencies. Whether and to what extent ignoring these dependencies affects the inferences drawn from such models remains to be assessed properly by future research.

A further limitation concerns the generalizability of correlations between influence and awareness tasks. These correlations are inherently task-specific and cannot be directly interpreted as correlations between influence and awareness constructs. This has been referred to as "task impurity" (Miyake et al., 2000), that is, no task can be a perfectly pure measure of a latent construct. With only one influence and one awareness task, we cannot aim to determine whether their relationship might generalize across different measures of the same construct. A promising alternative is to collect multiple awareness and influence measures and analyze them using generalized hierarchical factor models (Rey-Sáez, Franco-Martínez, Revuelta, et al., 2026; Rouder & Mehrvarz, 2026; Stevenson, Heathcote, et al., 2024; Stevenson, Innes, et al., 2024; Stevenson et al., 2025). These models adapt exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis to experimental settings, allowing researchers to model awareness and influence as latent factors underlying their respective measures and estimate the correlation between them. Their main advantage is that they do so by modeling trial-level responses within a hierarchical framework, as in our multilevel SDT model, but allowing for task-specific likelihoods (e.g., Bernoulli for binary responses or ex-Gaussian for response times). Moreover, combining multiple tasks can improve the precision of estimates of true correlations between task effects by leveraging the information each task shares with the others (Mehrvarz & Rouder, 2025; Rey-Sáez, Franco-Martínez, Revuelta, et al., 2026). This approach would allow researchers to move beyond task-specific associations and examine whether awareness and influence performance share common underlying processes across different paradigms.

Conclusion

Claims that information can be processed without conscious awareness have important implications for theories of human cognition. Yet such claims have often relied on inconsistent statistical evidence, small samples, few awareness trials, unreliable measures, and tests not suitable for evidence of absence. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence (Sagan, 1979), and we have shown that nonsignificant awareness effects, weak correlations, and significant regression intercepts can have much more ordinary methodological explanations, such as insufficient statistical power, differences in measurement scales, and measurement error. Clearly, the multilevel SDT model (like any statistical model) cannot compensate for insufficient data or invalid measures, but it provides a robust model-based approach to assessing the strength of evidence for and against unconscious processing while accounting for measurement error and differences in scale. We hope this framework, and its accessible implementation in the {uSDT} package, will encourage researchers to revisit established findings and design more informative studies capable of providing the robust evidence that claims of unconscious processing require.

decisions. In contextual-cuing paradigms, participants search for a target (a rotated T) among distractors (L-shaped), with some displays repeated across blocks (Old) and others presented for the first time (New). Contextual cuing was measured as the difference in RTs between Old and New displays (influence task), with faster responses to Old displays indicating learning. After the search task, participants completed an explicit recognition test (awareness task), identifying Old and New displays using a six-point confidence scale, allowing awareness to be assessed using both 𝑑 ′ and rating-based measures. For our illustration, we use Experiment 2 with a Spanish sample (𝑁 = 104), which included a relatively large number of trials for contextual-cuing research. Each participant completed 384 visual-search trials across 24 blocks (192 Old and 192 New), followed by 64 recognition trials (32 Old and 32 New), with responses ranging from 1 ("sure New") to 6 ("sure Old"). The data are publicly available at https://osf.io/jp3gx.

We fitted the multilevel SDT model to the trial-level data, following the original authors' preprocessing procedures. We excluded incorrect visual-search responses, RTs longer than 10 s, and RTs more than three standard deviations from each participant's mean (4.0% of trials).

Following Meyen et al. (2024), we dichotomized the remaining RTs at each participant's median, coding faster responses as "Old" responses (and slower as "New" responses). We considered Old displays as signal trials (and New displays as noise trials) to compute a 𝑑 ′ as the sensitivity of the influence measure. Recognition ratings were dichotomized into New (1-3) and Old (4-6) responses, with Old displays as signal trials. We fitted both frequentist and Bayesian models, using the latent regression parameterization for the latter, with a N (0, 1) prior on the intercept, a uniform prior on the correlation, and the default {uSDT} priors for the remaining parameters (see Appendix A). For comparison, we also applied the conventional two-step approach, testing the three hypotheses using a paired 𝑡 test, a Pearson correlation, and an ordinary least-squares regression intercept, respectively. Results are presented in Table 6.

The original analyses found a contextual-cuing effect, with responses 99 ms faster for Old than New displays, 𝑡 (103) = 10.02, 𝑝 < .001. However, recognition was also above chance (𝑑 ′ = 0.23, 𝑡 (103) = 6.95, 𝑝 < .001). Although not analysed in the original paper, the two-step analyses 2). Fitting the Multilevel SDT Model With {uSDT}

The code below fits the models of the contextual-cuing study of Vadillo et al. (2025), whose trial-level data are included in {uSDT}. The package takes the data of each task, one row per trial, and only needs to know which columns identify the participant, the condition, and the response.

RTs are split at each participant's median internally (Meyen et al., 2022).

library(uSDT) # Trial-level data of both tasks, one row per trial # Awareness measure # Influence measure data(vadillo_awareness) data(vadillo_cuing) #> subj condition judged.old #> subj condition rt #> 1 2001 old 0 #> 1 2001 new 1305.352 #> 2 2001 old 1 #> 2 2001 old 4027.887 #> 3 2001 new 1 #> 3 2001 old 2484.210 # Both tasks in one object, with Old displays as signal trials d <-usdt_data_tasks( awareness = vadillo_awareness, influence = vadillo_cuing, subject_col = "subj", condition_col = "condition", condition_levels = c(signal = "old", noise = "new"), response_col = list(awareness = "judged.old", influence = "rt"), response_levels = list(awareness = c(signal = 1, noise = 0), influence = c(signal = "faster", noise = "slower")), dichotomize = list(awareness = FALSE, influence = TRUE)) # Fit the frequentist hierarchical SDT model and check results fit <-hsdt(d); summary(fit) # Other utilities usdt_reliability(fit) # Reliability estimates per task and participant plot(fit, type = "roc") # Our figure 8 in main text plot(fit, type = "regression") # Our figures 9 and 10 in main text # Bayesian model: set prior distributions (if not, default priors used) priors <-usdt_priors(intercept = "normal(0, 1)", cor_dprime = "lkj(1)") # Fit the Bayesian hierarchical SDT model and check results fit_b <-hsdt(d, estimation = "bayesian", priors = priors, latent = "regression") summary(fit_b) # Bayes factors and plots for the same hypotheses as the frequentist model usdt_bf(fit_b) # Bayes factors and plot type as in Figure 11 usdt_bf(fit_b, hypothesis = c("rho = 0", "rho > 0"))

We use the term group-level dissociation hypothesis to refer collectively to simple and sensitivity dissociations, which represent two distinct criteria for establishing a dissociation between influence and awareness(Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006).

However, greater sensitivity in the influence task does not, by itself, establish unconscious processing. This interpretation relies on the assumption that the awareness task is at least as sensitive to consciously available information as the influence task. If this assumption holds, any additional sensitivity in the influence task cannot be explained by conscious information alone. To make this assumption more plausible,Reingold and Merikle (1988) recommended that the two tasks be as similar as possible, differing mainly in whether participants are explicitly asked to discriminate the relevant information.

For illustrative purposes, the RT distributions in Figure2are assumed to be normal with equal variances across conditions. Although empirical RT distributions are typically right-skewed, the same reasoning applies to asymmetric distributions, such as the lognormal.

This artifact applies to any score computed separately for each participant, whether a mean, a difference between means, a proportion of correct responses, a 𝑑 ′ , or parameters of a cognitive computational model, such as the drift rate of the drift diffusion model(Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).
